title: Imperfect Verbs
objectives: recognize the various forms (augments, stems, endings) of the imperfect active and middle/passive verbs,
predict how the augment will change with the various consonants, vowels, diphthongs and prepositional prefixes,
gain more practice in translating and working with Greek,
master 10 more high frequency vocabulary words,

content.text: In English we have only one official past tense (Tanya [[u]]drove[[/u]] the car.) This refers to time in the past.
If we want to refer to a continuous or repetitive act in the past, we may add a helping verb to a participle and say "Tanya [[u]]was driving[[/u]] the car."
In Greek, the [[u]]aorist[[/u]] tense is used to reference that the action of the verb simply happened in the past without regard to the exact time involved.
The [[u]]imperfect[[/u]] is used for showing continuity or repetitive action in the past. We will be working on the imperfect in this chapter.

learn.title: Learn Imperfect Indicative Verbs

content.text: The Greek imperfect tense is used when continuous or repeated action in the past is being referred to.
In English it will usually be translated with the helping verb was/were + the participle form of the verb (e.g. was singing).
Verbs that are deponent in the present tense are also deponent in the imperfect.
The imperfect is built from the present verb stem. It is preceded by an "ε" augment and followed by secondary active personal endings.

content.title: Imperfect Middle/Passive Indicative of λύω
content.note: The above paradigm is translated using the passive voice. The middle uses exactly the same forms, which would be translated—I was loosing (for myself), you were loosing (for yourself), he was loosing (for himself), etc. Context will determine whether the form should be translated middle or passive.

topics.title: Augments

content.text: The augment is added in 4 ways:

items.text:
before vowels the augment contracts with the vowel according to the following rules:
α + ε = η      ε + ε = η      ο + ε = ω
ει + ε = ῃ     αι + ε = ῃ     οι + ε = ῳ
αυ + ε = ηυ    ευ + ε = ηυ

below.label: Contraction Examples

content._layout_note: Each row prints rule, augmented form, lemma + "ε augment"; both Greek forms tap (hand cursors, rail walk p5).

below._disclosure: C1: chart payload behind an in-text "Examples" link (§6.1) -> accordion, §3.5 title. VERIFY-5H (l).

items.text:
Compound verbs with prepositions ending in a consonant: insert the augment between the prepositional prefix and the verb stem.
ἐκβάλλω becomes ἐξεβάλλον

Compound verbs with prepositions ending in a vowel: the final vowel of the preposition is dropped and the ε augment inserted in its place.
ἀποκτείνω becomes ἀπέκτεινον

content._disclosure: C5: "Augments (cont.)" continues the same numbered list 1-4 (the Augment Drill hint prints all four on one screen). VERIFY-5H (l).

topics._greek_note: Rule lines are bare font-Greek letters in the TBK (a,e,h,o,w,ei,ai,oi,au,eu); converted as notation, not taps.

content.title: ἔχω Imperfect Indicative
content.note: Note: This is an exception. The augment is a contraction of ε + ε = ει. Another exceptional augmented form is θέλω which takes an η becoming ἤθελεν in Mat 18:30.
